name: TV Shows
description: There are $$$n$$$ TV shows you want to watch. Suppose the whole time is split into equal parts called "minutes". The $$$i$$$-th of the shows is going from $$$l_i$$$-th to $$$r_i$$$-th minute, both ends inclusive. You need a TV to watch a TV show and you can't watch two TV shows which air at the same time on the same TV, so it is possible you will need multiple TVs in some minutes. For example, if segments $$$[l_i, r_i]$$$ and $$$[l_j, r_j]$$$ intersect, then shows $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ can't be watched simultaneously on one TV. Once you start watching a show on some TV it is not possible to "move" it to another TV (since it would be too distracting), or to watch another show on the same TV until this show ends. There is a TV Rental shop near you. It rents a TV for $$$x$$$ rupees, and charges $$$y$$$ ($$$y \lt x$$$) rupees for every extra minute you keep the TV. So in order to rent a TV for minutes $$$[a; b]$$$ you will need to pay $$$x + y \cdot (b - a)$$$. You can assume, that taking and returning of the TV doesn't take any time and doesn't distract from watching other TV shows. Find the minimum possible cost to view all shows. Since this value could be too large, print it modulo $$$10^9 + 7$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains integers $$$n$$$, $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^5$$$, $$$1 \le y \lt x \le 10^9$$$) — the number of TV shows, the cost to rent a TV for the first minute and the cost to rent a TV for every subsequent minute. Each of the next $$$n$$$ lines contains two integers $$$l_i$$$ and $$$r_i$$$ ($$$1 \le l_i \le r_i \le 10^9$$$) denoting the start and the end minute of the $$$i$$$-th TV show.
output_specification: Print exactly one integer — the minimum cost to view all the shows taken modulo $$$10^9 + 7$$$.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1061D — TV Shows [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
